claims.text: The studied material is a Mg–Ti–Zn lightweight high-entropy alloy produced by mechanical alloying followed by spark plasma sintering.
Mechanical alloying and SPS produce or preserve a non-equilibrium nanocrystalline structure in Mg–Ti–Zn alloys.
The as-sintered Mg–Ti–Zn structure is defect-rich.
The Mg–Ti–Zn alloy satisfies a density limit below 6 g/cm³.
The controlled comparison consists of as-sintered material and material annealed at 300°C or 600°C for 1 hour under inert atmosphere.
Annealing at 300°C largely preserves the metastable nanocrystalline features.
The as-sintered material has beneficial Mg enrichment at grain boundaries.
Mg-enriched grain boundaries promote rapid formation of a protective and adherent oxide barrier.
The protective oxide generated through Mg-enriched grain boundaries resists both corrosive attack and high-temperature oxidation.
Mg–Ti–Zn alloys made by ball milling and SPS can exhibit passivation and low corrosion current density.
Prior observations support grain-boundary chemistry as the cause of protective oxide formation in this alloy.
Annealing at 600°C causes significant grain growth in the Mg–Ti–Zn alloy.
Annealing at 600°C forms coarser equilibrium intermetallic phases in the Mg–Ti–Zn alloy.
Grain growth and intermetallic formation reduce the density of beneficial grain-boundary sites.
The loss of beneficial grain-boundary sites causes poorer oxide-scale adherence and increased corrosion rates.
Relative to the as-sintered baseline, 300°C annealing will lower corrosion current density in saline solution.
Relative to the as-sintered baseline, 300°C annealing will reduce oxide-scale spallation during oxidation at about 700°C.
The 600°C-annealed material will have higher corrosion current density and more oxide degradation than the 300°C-annealed material.
Porosity changes and non-uniform annealing temperature could confound the proposed structure–performance relationship.
